title: Spatial Audio: Foundations and Machine Learning Challenges
speaker: Boaz Rafaely
location: Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1, Jacob Ziskind Building
abstract: Spatial audio aims to capture and reproduce acoustic scenes while preserving the listener’s sense of direction, distance, and surrounding space. This seminar will introduce the foundations of spatial audio, including microphone array recording, Ambisonics representations and encoding, and binaural reproduction over headphones. We will then examine the challenges of recording spatial sound using a small number of microphones on wearable devices, highlighting recent approaches and the importance of perceptually motivated optimization. The talk will address speech enhancement using neural networks for spatial audio, including array agnostic approaches, the estimation of higher-order Ambisonics signals from low-order recordings, and preservation of spatial hearing cues when optimizing audio reproduction.BioBoaz Rafaely is a Professor at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev in Israel, where he leads the Acoustics Laboratory, conducting research in spatial audio signal processing. He has published over 200 papers in journals and conferences, and is the author of the book Fundamentals of Spherical Array Processing. Prof. Rafaely has previously served as Head of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at BGU, Chair of the Israeli Acoustical Association, and Chair of the Technical Committee on Audio Signal Processing of the European Acoustical Association. He has also been an associate editor for IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing, IEEE Signal Processing Letters, and Acta Acustica. He is an IEEE fellow

title: From Molecules to Macroscopic Devices: Advanced Carbon Nanotube Hybrids for Energy Applications
speaker: Haim Weissman
department: 2026-2027 Spotlight on Science Seminar Series - Dr. Haim Weissman (Department of Molecular Chemistry & Materials Science)
abstract: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) possess extraordinary strength and electrical conductivity. Nonetheless, CNT networks, constructed from dispersions, often suffer from inferior properties caused by nanotube bundling that limits their application in novel materials. In this talk, we will present our group’s supramolecular approach, utilizing perylene diimides (PDIs) and anthraquinones to achieve highly effective CNT dispersions in organic or aqueous solutions. We will demonstrate the application of these dispersions in the creation of robust, highly conductive buckypapers, advanced electrodes for energy materials, and transparent electrodes for next-generation flexible electronics. Ultimately, our work attempts to illustrate how mastering nanoscale interfacial chemistry provides a versatile platform for solving critical challenges in modern energy storage and transparent electronics technologies.

title: What Drives Trace Gas Emissions from Desert Soils: Biological, Chemical, or Biochemical Processes?
speaker: Ilya Gelfand
department: Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences
location: Seminar Room, Earth and Planetary Sciences Complex
abstract: Deserts cover nearly half of Earth’s land surface but remain among the least studied ecosystems with respect to trace gas fluxes. In particular, the processes controlling soil emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO), and methane (CH₄) are still poorly understood. In this talk, I will present recent field and laboratory results exploring how coupled biotic and abiotic processes regulate these gases in arid soils, focusing on two phenomena: the CO₂, N₂O, and NO pulse following rewetting of dry soil (the “Birch effect”) and CH₄ fluxes across dry and wet seasons. Using sensitive laser-based measurements and γ-irradiated (sterilized) soils, we show that post-wetting emissions of N₂O and NO occur within minutes of rewetting and are largely driven by abiotic reactions. The results indicate that ammonium (NH₄ ) is oxidized extracellularly to hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) by released enzymes such as ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), followed by rapid abiotic oxidation of NH₂OH to N₂O. This mechanism explains the immediate N₂O pulse observed in both live and sterilized soils and underscores the overlooked role of abiotic pathways in desert N₂O production. NO is also produced, but the mechanism of its production is not yet fully understood. In parallel, we conducted nearly continuous field measurements of CH₄ fluxes using automated chambers in the Negev Desert, Israel, across soils differing in carbon content. Contrary to the prevailing view that dry soils are consistent CH₄ sinks, we found that CH₄ was emitted about 75% of the time, with mean effluxes of 0.222 ± 0.007 nmol m ² s ¹ in summer and 0.081 ± 0.004 nmol m ² s ¹ in winter. A shading experiment reduced CH₄ emissions by 51%, suggesting that solar-driven abiotic reactions, rather than microbial processes, dominate CH₄ release. Together, these findings highlight that abiotic and enzyme-mediated processes can play a major role in trace gas dynamics of arid soils, especially under the intensifying drought–rewetting cycles projected for the future climate.

title: DNA Origami comes to age: Science and applications
speaker: Prof. Yuval Garini
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: DNA origami, invented over a decade ago, enables the construction of complex 2D and 3D nanostructures with programmable shapes. More recently, dynamic DNA origami systems have emerged, opening new opportunities in healthcare applications such as sensing, diagnostics, and targeted drug delivery. We developed a dynamic DNA origami nanocapsule for targeted drug delivery to stenotic arteries, addressing cardiovascular diseases, including atherothrombosis, which remain leading causes of death worldwide. The capsule encapsulates a clot-dissolving drug and autonomously releases it at stenotic sites in response to elevated shear forces generated by narrowed blood vessels. This approach may enable early intervention by paramedics, potentially improving current treatment strategies that rely on thrombolytic agents such as tPA, whose use is limited by bleeding risks. I will present the capsule design, synthesis, and structural characterization by AFM and electron microscopy. I will also discuss the mechanical characterization of the opening mechanism using optical tweezers.  See: H. title: Chevalley groups and their twisted analogues over rings: automorphisms and model theory
speaker: Elena Bunina
abstract:
Chevalley groups provide a common framework for classical matrix groups and exceptional groups over fields and rings. I will introduce ordinary and twisted Chevalley groups over commutative rings and discuss two related questions: how can we describe their automorphisms, and how much of the underlying ring can we recover from the group itself?

I will survey classification results for ordinary Chevalley groups and recent developments for their twisted analogues, highlighting the additional phenomena that arise in the twisted case. I will then turn to model theory, discussing the recovery of rings by first-order formulas, bi-interpretability, and consequences for elementary equivalence and axiomatizability. The emphasis will be on examples, main results, and the ideas linking the algebraic and logical approaches.

title: Faculty of Chemistry seminar
speaker: Prof. Oliver L.A. Monti
abstract: Materials for electronic devices of all kinds are dominated by a small set of materials whose properties are deeply understood and can be controlled with extraordinary precision. While the resulting electronics have arguably completely revolutionized society, there are now fundamental limitations in size, capability of integration into consumer-sized devices, and power efficiency. These limitations can only be overcome with completely new materials and device concepts, which in themselves require to go beyond charge current as information carrier. In this talk, I will introduce the notion of spin as a natural choice for low-power electronics. I will show how “small molecule” organic semiconductors can be used to tailor spintronic responses, on timescales of 10-15 s, length scales of ~10 Å and energy scales of molecular vibrations or less. Interfaces between such molecules and a wide variety of electronic materials permit conversion of charge to spin, selective spin injection or control of the spin degrees of freedom. The origin of these effects stems from the formation of a hybrid molecular interface, a chemical entity that extends beyond either the molecular material or its counterpart, enabling new ways of designing materials platforms for ultraefficient electronics.

title: Local Support Learning
speaker: Assaf Ben Kish
location: Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1, Jacob Ziskind Building
abstract: Modern neural networks learn in phases: large-scale pretraining followed by smaller finetuning phases. Catastrophic forgetting hurts this process, as each new phase can overwrite capabilities acquired in prior ones. First, we show that gradient updates, whether produced by SGD, Adam, or Muon, are inherently suboptimal for retaining prior capabilities. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Local Support Learning (LSL), a general-purpose learning framework that augments gradient-based training for retention of prior capabilities without access to prior data. During a new learning phase, LSL pairs two components with distinct roles: a standard weight adapter, trained as usual to minimize the loss, and a special gate based on a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) that enables the adapter only on inputs from the current phase's training distribution. Throughout multi-phase training, LSL retains 99% of prior performance while learning at full capacity, and shows favorable scaling trends in LLMs of up to 7B parameters. We complement these results with a theoretical analysis explaining why MLP-based gates are not well suited for this framework, while density estimators such as GMMs achieve near-perfect retention.Bio:Assaf Ben-Kish is a PhD student at Tel Aviv University, interested in understanding the fundamentals of learning. His work investigates deep neural networks, drawing inspiration from biological learning systems. Assaf is advised by Prof. Raja Giryes and is currently also a research intern at NVIDIA. Previously, he was a visiting student researcher in the Spoken Language Systems group at MIT CSAIL.

title: On the isotropic boundary of the ample cone of a hyperkähler manifold
speaker: Amerik Ekaterina
abstract: It follows from an old result of Kovacs that the ample cone of a projective K3 surface of Picard number at least three is either“round” (equal to the positive cone), or has “no round part”, that isthe boundary of the ample cone does not contain any open subset of the isotropic cone (and is actually nowhere dense in the isotropic cone).With the help of hyperbolic geometry, this easily generalizes to the hyperkähler case.We pursue this a bit further and prove that any real analytic curve in the projectivization of the isotropic boundary of the ample cone of a projective hyperkähler manifold lies in a sphere contained in this isotropic boundary.We discuss how the union of maximal such spheres, the “Apollonian carpet”, equal to the union of all analytic curves on the projectivized isotropic boundary, can loo like.Actually, the phenomena discussed are already visible in the world of K3 surfaces; we provide some K3 examples.

title: Physics Colloquium : "The optics of life - The materials and physics behind biogenic structural colors and its biomimetics"
speaker: Dan Oron, Weizmann
location: Place:     Levin building, Lecture Hall No. 8
abstract: Light is the source of life on Earth, and is used in numerous ways in the plant and animal kingdoms for a variety of applications, including photosynthesis, vision, camouflage, communication, thermal management and more. As such, evolution has led to the creation of intricate optical systems with highly controlled and regulated properties. The talk will present an overview of some of these unique optical systems, focusing on the ubiquitous guanine-based optical reflectors and on more recently discovered 3D structural color systems. In particular, correlated optical and structural characterization will be shown to unearth new information about the function of some of the more poorly understood biological light manipulation systems and to reveal clues about their evolution. Finally, the potential for previously unexplored bioinspired optics based on these findings will be discussed.

title: A CURIOUS CASE OF PNICTOGEN CATIONS
speaker: Prof. Roman Dobrovetsky
affiliation: School of Chemistry, Tel Aviv University, Israel
abstract: Group 15 species have attracted considerable attention for their potential to activate small molecules and mediate catalytic transformations. In particular, structurally constrained pnictogen centers have emerged as promising platforms for transition-metal-like reactivity. Our research focuses on structurally constrained Pn(III) and Pn(V) cations (Pn = pnictogen), which exhibit distinct but complementary reactivity patterns. As we have recently demonstrated for P(III) systems, structural constraint can promote ambiphilic small-molecule activation and transition-metal-mimicking catalysis. In contrast, P(V) cations can exhibit exceptional Lewis acidity, enabling small-molecule activation and catalytic transformations. In this talk, I will highlight the potential of structurally constrained pnictogen cations as versatile platforms for small-molecule activation and catalysis, presenting recent advances in the chemistry of these species. These include H2 activation and metallomimetic catalytic hydrogenation mediated by constrained P(III) cations, C–Si bond activation by a structurally constrained Sb(III) cation followed by catalytic silane redistribution, and the development of novel P(V)-based Lewis superacids and their reactivity toward small molecules.

title: Central Limit Theorems for Finitary Factors of iid Processes
speaker: Nicolò Paviato
abstract:
Given a Z^d-subshift with an invariant probability measure, we study statistical limit theorems for the Birkhoff sums of regular observables. Although the literature for d = 1 is well developed, for Z^d-actions with d ≥ 2 the theory is much less understood. In this talk, we present our techniques to study such systems under the assumption that they are finitary factors of iid processes with suitable coding radius estimates. We prove a central limit theorem with rates of convergence and a functional limit theorem with a Brownian-sheet limit. Our results can be applied to classical models in statistical mechanics, such as the Ising model, proper colourings, and the hard-core model, among others.

This is joint work with Prof. Zemer Kosloff and Prof. Raimundo Briceño.

title: Spatial self-organization and oxygen field dynamics of multispecies aerobic bacteria
speaker: Prof. Joel Stavans
affiliation: Department of Physics of Complex Systems, Weizmann Institute
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: The appearance of oxygen on Earth following the Great Oxygenation Event 2.4 Gya ago and its gradual rise to modern levels brought profound changes on extant life and its spatial organization. This is true of bacterial communities in various ecosystems, from soil, sediments and microbial mats, to the fresh-water column and the oceans. Oxytactic motile bacteria swim following oxygen gradients, and in suspension near a air-liquid interface can drive self-organized, collective coherent flows called bioconvection, whose spatial scales exceed the cell size by orders of magnitude. I will present results of bioconvection experiments with multispecies suspensions of wild-type bacteria collected from the pristine hyper-diverse bacterial communities of Cuatro Ciénegas, Coahuila, Mexico, whose origin dates back to the pre-Cambrian. Our results demonstrate a plethora of amazing dynamical behaviors, including spatial segregation between different species. This segregation takes place despite enhanced mixing by the hydrodynamic flow and in the absence of antagonistic interactions between species. Using space-resolved optical oxygen detection methods, we visualized the oxygen field directly for the first time, shedding light on the tight interplay between oxygen gradients and local bacterial concentrations. Furthermore, we modulated the oxygen concentration in the air above air-water interfaces and demonstrate the fundamental role this parameter plays in setting the behavior of bioconvection, and in the auto-organization of different bacterial species, as a function of distance from the interface. The combination of oxygen consumption and preference between species is key to understanding the high diversity of species-dependent bioconvective patterns, dynamical  spatial segregation in suspensions, as well as the self-organization of species in the aerobic sector of microbial mats. Theoretical modelling recapitulates differences in bioconvective patterns among species and provides support for a mechanism behind segregation. abstract: An idea, a test tube, an animal experiment, a patient. That journey usually takes years. Our center helps make it possible faster. Part of my work is building optical imaging systems to study blood flow in the brain and help doctors monitor skin grafts in the clinic. Now AI is changing the pace of our work. A year of software development can now take a week, sometimes only a day. Ideas arrive faster than we can test them. Could computer simulations help us keep up? From 3D-printed tools for experiments to virtual physiology and even simulations in computational psychiatry, I will share what surprised us, where simulation can spare animals, and where it cannot. Can our ability to test keep pace with our ability to create? It can, with the right crew.

title: Restoring the balance: mechanics of differentiation and regeneration in the mammalian inner ear
speaker: Prof. David Sprinzak
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: The mammalian hearing and balance systems rely on specialized sensory hair cells that convert sound waves and head movements to electrical signals in our brain. These hairs cells are located within sensory domains where each sensory hair cell is surrounded by non-sensory supporting cells, forming a checkerboard-like pattern. Many non-mammalian species like fish and birds have the capability to regenerate lost hair cells by the proliferation and differentiation of nearby supporting cells. In contrast, in mammals the capacity to regenerate hair cells exists at early postnatal stage, but quickly diminishes after birth. Little is known about the local factors underlying the decision to trans-differentiate and the reasons for the decline in regeneration capacity with age. We combine live imaging of mouse inner ear explants and biophysical modelling to elucidate the local signaling and mechanical cues that regulate differentiation and regeneration of hair cells. We reveal unexpected age-dependent dynamic patterning processes that deviate from the classical models describing the differentiation of hair cells and supporting cells. We find that mechanical stress in the sensory domains changes with age and that perturbing it alters the observed differentiation patterns. A biophysical model incorporating local mechanical regulation of intercellular signaling captures both hair cell differentiation and regeneration patterns across ages. Together, these findings identify mechanical stress as a crucial regulator of hair cell differentiation and support an underlying mechanism in which the interplay between local mechanics and signaling shapes regenerative responses. This coupling offers a framework for understanding the age-dependent decline in hair cell regeneration and motivates investigation of mechanical regulation as a potential therapeutic target for hearing and balance disorders. title: Good Karma: The Computational Lens and Society
speaker: Prof. Omer Reingold
abstract: As computation changes how we live, work, and make decisions about one another, understanding and helping shape its societal impact is part of the professional responsibility of theoretical computer scientists. This responsibility extends across the many areas our field touches and a multitude of societal concerns. We also have something powerful to contribute: the computational lens often transforms our understanding of long-standing notions such as secrecy, knowledge, privacy, fairness, and incentives. Theory helps us formulate difficult questions, uncover hidden obstacles, and discover new possibilities. Sometimes this work comes with a pleasant bonus: deep theory and applications we had no idea we were looking for. Call it good karma. We will explore this exchange through algorithmic fairness. How can we make predictions that serve people well across the many overlapping groups they belong to? Following this question has led to ideas such as multicalibration and outcome indistinguishability, connecting fairness to learning, statistics, and complexity theory. Along the way, efforts to address discrimination have shed light on the meaning of individual probabilities and produced new approaches to robust learning with uses well beyond fairness. We will then turn to the foundations of AI alignment. How can we train and supervise systems whose capabilities may exceed our ability to evaluate their work? Here, even finding the right questions requires substantial creativity. The experience with cryptography, privacy, computational game theory and algorithmic fairness offers reasons to take on this challenge with ambition. We can also expect that, by doing work that matters, we will also discover deep theory we did not know we were missing.

department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: As epithelial development or wound closure approaches completion, cell proliferation progressively slows via contact inhibition of proliferation (CIP)—a mechanism understood as being strictly local. Here we report the discovery of inhibition of proliferation through an unanticipated mechanism that is non-local. As a confluent epithelial layer becomes progressively more jammed, two interpenetrating networks emerge: islands of mechanically compressed non-cycling cells growing within an ocean of mechanically tensed cycling cells. The evolution of the compression network was found to be susceptible to both specific molecular stimuli and injury-induced unjamming. Interestingly, despite these perturbations, the size distribution of compressed islands consistently followed a power law with a cutoff that shifted toward larger island sizes as the network developed. This behavior was accompanied by a characteristic length scale that diverged as the system approached, but never crossed, the percolation threshold. These features were well captured by preferential network simulations. Together, these findings demonstrate the existence of a network-based inhibition of proliferation (NIP) that is self-organizing and poised in proximity to criticality. Finally, I will discuss emerging directions aimed at uncovering the mechanical origins of intracellular compression and how local cell divisions and mechanical interactions drive the self-organization of compressed-cell networks.

title: Physiological Invariance: Lessons from Excitability
speaker: Prof. Shimon Marom
affiliation: Department of Physiology, Biophysics and Systems Biology, Technion
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: An excitable cell produces a stereotyped electrical response reliably over long periods, while the molecular composition that realizes this response varies widely between cells and, over time, within each cell. Because its biophysics, biochemistry, mathematics, and physiological function are comparatively well understood, excitability offers a model system for studying such invariance. Beginning with a self-contained introduction and drawing on theory and experiment, the lecture proceeds from point systems to spatially extended ones, examines the low-dimensional relations that sustain function, considers the energetic cost of the many configurations that realize it, and traces the routes by which a cell moves among them.  the latest updates and content on Soft Matter and Biological Physics at the Weizmann Institute, visit our website.  Website Link  Please register for our new mailing list, even if you have already registered in the past.
